verses.bibleText: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The words “For this cause” reach back to the close of chapter 2. Gentile believers who were once strangers to the covenants have been brought near by Christ’s blood, reconciled with Jewish believers in one body, made members of God’s household, and built together into a dwelling place for God. Paul is about to pray that this new community will experience inwardly what God has already accomplished for it in Christ. Yet the mention of his imprisonment leads him into a lengthy explanation of his Gentile ministry, and the prayer is not resumed until verse 14.

Paul was physically a prisoner of Rome, but he calls himself “the prisoner of Jesus Christ.” Rome could confine his body, yet it did not define the meaning of his circumstances. His chains had arisen from Christ’s commission to carry the gospel to the Gentiles. The fierce reaction to that mission, especially when Paul spoke openly of being sent to the nations, contributed directly to his arrest and prolonged imprisonment.

“For you Gentiles” does not place blame upon the readers. It interprets Paul’s suffering as service on their behalf. He had defended their right to enter God’s people through faith in Christ without becoming Jewish proselytes, and he had accepted the consequences of that witness. His sufferings possess no atoning value alongside Christ’s unique sacrifice; they are the costly obedience of a servant whose message rests entirely upon the cross.

The unfinished sentence itself carries emotional force. Paul begins to pray, remembers his chains, and pauses to reassure the Gentiles that neither his imprisonment nor their inclusion in the church is an accident. What appears outwardly to be defeat belongs within Christ’s mission. Earthly powers may hinder a messenger, but they cannot imprison the gospel or overturn the purpose of the risen Lord.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes one who is bound or imprisoned. Although Paul was held under Roman authority, he identifies himself as Christ’s prisoner because his chains resulted from obedience to Christ’s commission and remained under Christ’s sovereign rule.

verses.bibleText: If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul assumes that the readers have heard about the stewardship entrusted to him. The expression “If ye have heard” is not best read as though he seriously doubts their knowledge. It resembles a courteous reminder: surely they know something of the responsibility God placed upon him for their benefit. Because Ephesians may have circulated among several congregations, some hearers may have known Paul personally while others knew his ministry only through reports.

The KJV’s “dispensation” translates a word drawn from household administration. Chapter 2 has just described believers as members of God’s household, and Paul now identifies himself as one who has received a responsibility within that household. He did not invent its membership requirements or possess authority to exclude people according to personal preference. The Master of the house entrusted him with the administration of grace toward the Gentiles.

“The grace of God” includes the gospel Paul proclaimed, but it also describes the commission itself. Being entrusted with ministry was not a reward for personal worthiness. Paul had once persecuted the church and resisted the name he now preached. God’s decision to transform such a man into an apostle to the nations displayed the very grace Paul was sent to announce.

The phrase “given me to you-ward” keeps ministry directed outward. Spiritual gifts and responsibilities are not private marks of superiority. They are entrusted for the salvation, instruction, unity, and growth of others. Paul’s apostleship was distinctive and foundational, yet the same principle applies to every gift Christ gives His church: grace received becomes grace administered in service.

wordNotes.term: If ye have heard — εἴ γε ἠκούσατε (ei ge ēkousate)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression ordinarily assumes that the condition is true: “if indeed,” or “surely you have heard.” It need not imply serious doubt. The wording may reflect the broad audience of the letter, some of whom knew Paul mainly by reputation.

The word describes household management, stewardship, or an administrative responsibility. Here it refers to Paul’s God-given responsibility to administer the message of grace to the Gentiles, rather than primarily to a period of history.

verses.bibleText: How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; (as I wrote afore in few words,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The commission described in verse 2 rested upon divine revelation. God made the mystery known to Paul; Paul did not discover it by intellectual brilliance, political calculation, or gradual accommodation to Gentile culture. His encounter with the risen Christ overturned his former understanding and placed him under a commission to carry Christ’s name to the nations.

“Mystery” does not describe teaching that must remain obscure. The word marks the contrast between what was once hidden in God’s purpose and what has now been disclosed. Religious movements in the ancient world often guarded secret rites for a privileged inner circle. The Christian mystery moves in the opposite direction: once revealed, it is preached openly to every nation. Its center is Christ, and its particular emphasis here is the equal incorporation of believing Jews and Gentiles into one body.

Paul adds, “as I wrote afore in few words.” He most likely refers to what he has already written in this letter, especially the gathering of all things in Christ in Ephesians 1:9-10 and the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles in Ephesians 2:11-22. No lost document is required. The earlier paragraphs stated the mystery briefly; the present section explains Paul’s responsibility in its proclamation.

The revelation given to Paul did not exalt him as the center of the message. It made him a servant of Christ’s purpose. Genuine revelation humbles the recipient because its source is God, its content is Christ, and its goal is the blessing of others. Paul’s authority therefore rests neither in personal charisma nor in hidden knowledge, but in the risen Lord who revealed His saving purpose and commissioned its public announcement.

wordNotes.explanation: Revelation is an uncovering or disclosure initiated by God. Paul’s understanding of the Gentile mission did not arise from speculation or social convenience but from God’s self-disclosure centered in Jesus Christ.
In Paul, a mystery is not an unintelligible secret reserved for religious elites. It is a divine purpose formerly hidden but now revealed and publicly proclaimed through the gospel.

verses.bibleText: Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A publicly read letter enables the churches to recognize Paul’s God-given understanding. Apostolic revelation is not left as an unverifiable claim about a private experience. It is expressed in words, read aloud in the congregation, examined in relation to the gospel, and made available to the whole church.

“My knowledge” is better understood as Paul’s insight rather than as information he produced independently. The preceding verse has already identified God as the One who made the mystery known. Paul can speak confidently about his understanding without boasting because both the revelation and the ability to communicate it are gifts of grace.

“The mystery of Christ” is the revealed purpose centered in Christ and accomplished through Him. The expression includes the larger plan to gather all things under Christ, but the immediate focus is His creation of one reconciled people from Jews and Gentiles. The mystery is therefore both Christological and communal: Christ is not merely the subject of individual devotion but the One in whom former enemies become one body.

The verse also assumes that careful reading produces understanding. The mystery has depth, but it is not deliberately obscure. The Spirit who revealed it through the apostles also gave the church a written witness through which its meaning could be heard, studied, and obeyed.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun refers to understanding, comprehension, or insight. Paul’s insight was given through revelation, yet the readers could recognize and understand it by hearing his written explanation.

verses.bibleText: Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Israel’s Scriptures plainly announced that the nations would be blessed. God promised Abraham that all families of the earth would find blessing through him. The prophets looked toward the nations coming to God’s light, worshiping the Lord, and sharing in the salvation He would reveal. Paul therefore cannot mean that every aspect of Gentile salvation had been entirely absent from earlier revelation.

What earlier generations did not see was the precise form that fulfillment would take. Believing Gentiles would not enter as subordinate dependents of a nationally restored Israel, nor would they first need to become Jewish proselytes. Through Christ they would stand beside believing Jews as equal heirs, equal members of one body, and equal participants in the promise. The cross would remove the hostility, and the Spirit would inhabit the united community. That radical equality is the mystery described in the following verse.

The words “as it is now revealed” may compare the present fullness of disclosure with earlier partial anticipation. Verse 9 nevertheless emphasizes that the completed plan had remained hidden in God. The promises were present; their surprising realization in one new humanity became clear only through Christ’s death, resurrection, and the Spirit’s work among Jews and Gentiles.

The revelation came to Christ’s “holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.” Holy means set apart for God’s purpose, not morally incapable of error in every personal decision. Peter, for example, needed correction when his conduct compromised the gospel’s implications. Yet the apostles and prophets possessed a foundational role as recipients and heralds of the revealed mystery. Their witness, preserved in Scripture, remains normative for the church.

The Spirit is the divine revealer. Human prejudice would not naturally have produced this community of equals, and religious tradition alone could easily have resisted it. The same Spirit who disclosed the mystery also demonstrated its truth by being poured out upon uncircumcised Gentile believers. God Himself testified that they were accepted through faith in Christ.

wordNotes.term: as it is now revealed — ὡς νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη (hōs nyn apekalyphtē)
wordNotes.explanation: The wording contrasts earlier generations with the present era of fulfillment. The Old Testament anticipated blessing for the nations, but the complete equality of believing Gentiles and Jews in one body has now been disclosed with a clarity and reality not previously possessed.

wordNotes.term: apostles and prophets — ἀπόστολοι καὶ προφῆται (apostoloi kai prophētai)
wordNotes.explanation: The pair most naturally refers to Christ’s foundational New Testament witnesses, already mentioned in Ephesians 2:20. Through the Spirit they received and proclaimed the authoritative revelation upon which the church was established.

verses.bibleText: That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here the mystery is stated directly. It is not simply that Gentiles may be saved. The Old Testament had already promised blessing for the nations. The newly revealed wonder is that believing Gentiles become “fellowheirs,” members “of the same body,” and “partakers” of the promise together with believing Jews. Paul places three emphatic “together-with” words beside one another so that no idea of second-class membership can survive.

As fellowheirs, Gentile believers share the inheritance promised to God’s people. That inheritance includes present adoption, the Spirit as its pledge, and the future kingdom in which the redeemed will receive resurrection life and inhabit the renewed creation. It is not restricted to an earthly territory under present conditions of sin and death. In Christ the promise given through Abraham opens toward the restoration of all things under God’s reign.

Being “of the same body” is stronger than peaceful coexistence between two permanently separate peoples. Christ has created one new humanity and reconciled both groups to God through the cross. Jewish believers do not lose their history, and Gentile believers do not become ethnically Jewish. Their differences are placed within a deeper identity: together they constitute the body whose Head is Christ.

As fellow partakers, they share “his promise in Christ.” The promise belongs neither to ancestry nor to ceremonial status as an independent possession. It is held in Christ, the promised Seed and the One in whom every divine blessing is secured. Participation therefore comes “by the gospel”—through hearing the good news, believing in Christ, and being united with Him by the Spirit.

No circumcision, food regulation, festival, or national boundary can be added as an entrance requirement. Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice fulfilled the typological system that anticipated Him, and His blood created peace between those formerly divided. The moral demand of love and holiness has not disappeared; the second half of Ephesians will press it urgently. Yet obedience is now the Spirit-produced life of those already accepted in Christ, not a means of purchasing membership in God’s family.

The mystery confronts every form of spiritual superiority. Race, culture, religious heritage, social standing, and human accomplishment cannot establish degrees of nearness to God. All believers approach through the same Christ, receive the same Spirit, belong to the same body, and await the same inheritance.

wordNotes.term: fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers — συγκληρονόμα, σύσσωμα, συμμέτοχα (synklēronoma, syssōma, symmetocha)
wordNotes.explanation: All three words begin with the idea of “together with.” Gentile believers are heirs together with Jewish believers, incorporated together in one body, and sharers together in the promise. The repeated compounds emphasize complete equality rather than secondary membership.
The promise gathers up the blessing pledged through Abraham, the promised gift of the Spirit, and the inheritance that will be fully received in God’s restored creation.

verses.bibleText: Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The gospel made Paul a servant. He did not appoint himself, inherit the office through social standing, or earn it through religious achievement. The passive wording—“I was made a minister”—keeps the initiative with God.

His ministry arose “according to the gift of the grace of God.” Paul had been a zealous persecutor of the church and an opponent of the very Gentile inclusion he now proclaimed. Transforming him into Christ’s messenger displayed grace in a particularly striking form. The commission was undeserved, but it was not unreal or ineffective. Grace both forgave Paul and redirected his life into costly service.

The gift was given “by the effectual working of his power.” The power in view is the divine power celebrated throughout Ephesians—the power displayed in Christ’s resurrection and exaltation. It changed Paul’s allegiance, overcame his former hostility, and sustained his witness despite opposition. His imprisonment did not indicate that the power had ceased. Divine power was operating through a servant whose outward circumstances looked weak.

Ministry therefore cannot become a ground for boasting. The message belongs to Christ, the capacity comes from God, and the results depend upon the Spirit. The servant remains responsible for faithfulness and labor, but even diligent labor is the outworking of grace. Such dependence does not weaken service; it frees the minister from pretending that human ability can accomplish spiritual creation.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means a servant or one who performs service on behalf of another. Paul’s ministry placed him under the authority of the gospel and its Lord rather than making the gospel his personal possession.

wordNotes.term: effectual working of his power — ἐνέργεια τῆς δυνάμεως (energeia tēs dynameōs)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression describes divine power put into effective operation. God’s power transformed Paul from a persecutor into a gospel servant and continued sustaining his ministry amid weakness and imprisonment.

verses.bibleText: Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Memory of grace shapes Paul’s estimate of himself. He calls himself “less than the least of all saints,” likely recalling the violence with which he had once pursued Christ’s people. The expression is not theatrical self-contempt. Paul knows that he is an apostle and speaks with the authority of his commission. Yet he never interprets that commission as evidence that he deserved it.

Grace does more than pardon the past. It entrusts the forgiven sinner with a new vocation. The former persecutor was commissioned to announce Christ among those he once would have excluded. Paul’s ministry therefore became a living illustration of his message: God reconciles enemies, destroys hostility, and creates servants from rebels.

The content of his preaching is “the unsearchable riches of Christ.” These riches include redemption through His blood, forgiveness, adoption, peace with God, reconciliation across human divisions, the gift of the Spirit, access to the Father, victory over hostile powers, and the promised inheritance. Every blessing named in the opening chapters is found in Christ rather than in human merit.

“Unsearchable” does not mean that nothing can be known. Paul was sent precisely to preach these riches. They can be known truly without being known exhaustively. No generation will reach the point at which Christ’s grace has been fully explored or His sufficiency exhausted. The gospel is simple enough to be received by faith and deep enough to occupy the redeemed throughout eternity.

Paul’s humility and confidence therefore belong together. He is small in his own estimation because grace is great, yet he speaks boldly because the riches he announces are Christ’s. Remembered sin keeps the servant humble; experienced mercy keeps him from despair; the inexhaustible Christ keeps the message abundant.

wordNotes.explanation: The unusual expression intensifies Paul’s sense of unworthiness. It reflects his remembered persecution of the church rather than a denial of the grace, authority, or calling God had given him.
The adjective describes something whose tracks cannot be completely traced. Christ’s riches can be truly proclaimed and received, but they can never be exhaustively mapped or depleted.

verses.bibleText: And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
What had been hidden is now to be brought into the light. Paul’s assignment was not limited to announcing salvation to Gentiles; he was also to help everyone see the meaning and outworking of God’s revealed purpose. Jews and Gentiles alike needed to understand that the gospel creates a shared life in Christ and that no former group possesses superior covenant standing.

The KJV speaks of “the fellowship of the mystery.” An important textual variation gives the sense “the administration of the mystery.” The two ideas meet within the chapter. God has ordered a plan in which former outsiders become fellowheirs, and those brought into that plan share a new fellowship in one body. Paul illuminates both the divine arrangement and the community it produces.

The mystery had been hidden “from the beginning of the world” in God. It was not preserved in a secret human tradition or guarded by angelic intermediaries. It belonged to the Creator’s own counsel until the appointed time of revelation. Salvation in Christ was therefore no emergency repair conceived after all other approaches failed. God’s purpose to overcome sin and unite His people in the Son preceded its historical disclosure.

Calling God the One “who created all things” broadens the horizon. The reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles is one part of a plan as wide as creation. The Creator who made humanity is restoring humanity, and the One who made all things will finally gather all things under Christ. This eternal purpose does not make God the author of sin; it reveals that rebellion never caught Him without a saving answer.

The KJV’s concluding phrase, “by Jesus Christ,” harmonizes with the wider witness of Scripture. The Son is not a creature within the universe. All things came into being through Him. The Christ who reconciles the nations is the divine Creator through whom humanity first received life and through whom creation will be restored.

wordNotes.term: fellowship of the mystery — κοινωνία / οἰκονομία (koinōnia / oikonomia)
wordNotes.explanation: The textual tradition underlying the KJV reads “fellowship,” stressing shared participation in the revealed mystery. Many early Greek witnesses read “administration” or “plan.” The context includes both God’s ordering of the mystery and the shared life created through it.

wordNotes.term: by Jesus Christ — διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (dia Iēsou Christou)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase appears in the manuscript tradition followed by the KJV but is absent from several early witnesses. The truth it expresses is firmly taught elsewhere: the eternal Son is the divine agent through whom all created things came into existence.

verses.bibleText: To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The horizon widens from the nations on earth to the spiritual realm. God’s purpose is that His manifold wisdom should become known “by the church” to rulers and authorities in heavenly places. The church is therefore more than the recipient of salvation. By its very existence, it becomes a living demonstration of what God has accomplished through Christ.

“Manifold” portrays wisdom in richly varied form. God did not overcome the divisions produced by sin by making every person culturally identical. He joined diverse people in one body, preserving their humanity while removing the hostility and spiritual hierarchy that separated them. The united church is like an intricately patterned work whose varied elements reveal the wisdom of its Maker.

Within Ephesians, “principalities and powers” most naturally includes the hostile spiritual forces later identified as the church’s enemies. These powers had participated in a world of rebellion, deception, domination, and division. They could point to human hostility as evidence of sin’s apparent success. The reconciled community now answers them. Jews and Gentiles worshiping one Father through one Lord in one Spirit announce that the cross has created peace and that the powers’ divisive rule is doomed.

Christ has already been exalted above every principality and power. Believers have been raised with Him, although conflict continues until His victory is fully manifested. The church’s witness to the powers is therefore not boastful triumphalism. Its authority comes entirely from union with the crucified and risen Christ. The community that bears this witness remains dependent upon grace and must still put on God’s armor against spiritual attack.

The statement gives ordinary church life cosmic significance. Reconciliation across racial, national, social, and cultural barriers is not merely good public policy. It displays before the universe the power and wisdom of God. Conversely, cherished prejudice and spiritual superiority obscure the truth the church was created to proclaim.

This cosmic witness fits the larger biblical conflict between Christ and the powers of evil. Heavenly intelligences observe God’s redemptive work, while hostile powers encounter in the church a sign of their coming judgment. The church does not defeat evil by its own institutional strength. It bears witness to the victory Christ has already won and lives in anticipation of the day when every opposing power will be finally removed.

wordNotes.explanation: The rare adjective describes rich variety or many-sided complexity, like an intricately patterned or multicolored work. God’s wisdom is displayed through the surprising way He creates unity without erasing the diversity of His redeemed people.

wordNotes.term: principalities and powers — ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι (archai kai exousiai)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression denotes spiritual rulers and authorities. Within Ephesians it most likely points especially to hostile powers opposed to God, though the wider heavenly audience of God’s work need not be excluded.

verses.bibleText: According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Nothing in this plan is improvised. The church’s creation, the equality of Jews and Gentiles, and the witness borne to the heavenly powers unfold “according to the eternal purpose” of God. Human rebellion did not force God to surrender His intention for creation or search uncertainly for a remedy.

The purpose was “purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord.” The underlying verb can carry the sense of accomplishing or carrying out. What God determined before the ages entered history through Jesus the Messiah. His incarnation, obedient life, atoning death, resurrection, exaltation, and continuing lordship brought the ancient purpose into effect.

The full title is significant. Jesus is the Christ, the promised and anointed King in whom Israel’s hope reaches fulfillment. He is also “our Lord,” possessing authority over the church and over every cosmic power. The mystery is not an abstract principle of universal togetherness; it is unity created under the lordship of Jesus and through His reconciling blood.

God’s eternal purpose should not be confused with the idea that He caused sin or rendered human choices unreal. Scripture holds rebellious creatures responsible for their decisions. The assurance is that evil cannot finally overthrow God’s design. Before the conflict unfolded in history, God had already purposed that creation would find its restoration and unity in His Son.

wordNotes.term: eternal purpose — πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων (prothesis tōn aiōnōn)
wordNotes.explanation: Literally a purpose associated with or established before the ages, the phrase describes God’s enduring redemptive intention rather than a temporary response to changing circumstances.

verses.bibleText: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Union with Christ gives believers “boldness and access with confidence.” In the ancient world, unrestricted access to a king or high official was rare and carefully controlled. Ephesians has already declared that people once alienated from God now approach the Father together through Christ and in one Spirit. Here that access becomes personal and prayerful.

Boldness is not irreverence. It is the freedom to speak openly because the worshiper has been welcomed. Sin naturally produces fear, concealment, and distance. Christ’s atoning death removes condemnation for the believer, and His living mediation assures continuing access to the Father. No human priesthood, ethnic privilege, or personal merit is needed to supplement Him.

The sacrifice that opened this access was offered once for all. Its sufficiency is complete and cannot be repeated or improved. The risen Christ nevertheless continues His heavenly ministry as the believer’s Mediator and High Priest. Because He lives in God’s presence on behalf of His people, they may draw near for mercy, grace, cleansing, and strength.

The KJV speaks of access “by the faith of him.” The phrase can be understood as faith in Christ or as a reference to His faithfulness. The immediate emphasis most likely falls upon believers’ faith in Him, as the similar wording in verse 17 suggests. Yet their faith has value only because its object is the faithful Christ, whose obedience and sacrifice established the way to God.

Confidence therefore rests outside the worshiper’s fluctuating feelings. A believer may come with grief, weakness, confession, or perplexity and still speak freely before the Father. The open door is Christ Himself. Faith enters that door with reverence, gratitude, and assurance that the Father hears.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes freedom or openness of speech. In prayer it describes the privilege of speaking honestly before God without the fear of rejection, because acceptance rests in Christ.
The noun can describe being brought into the presence of a ruler. Through Christ, believers are introduced into the Father’s presence and welcomed there with confidence.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The thought of his chains might have discouraged the churches. If Paul truly carried a divine commission, why had he remained imprisoned for years? Why did the herald of Christ’s cosmic victory appear powerless before earthly authorities? Paul asks the readers not to judge God’s purpose by outward appearances.

The grammar permits more than one interpretation, but the flow most naturally means that Paul is asking them not to lose heart. His tribulations had come through faithfulness to the Gentile mission described in the preceding verses. They were not signs that Christ had abandoned him or that the Gentiles’ place in the church was uncertain.

Paul calls these sufferings “your glory.” His endurance had helped bring the gospel to the nations, and those who believed had received forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, and the promised inheritance. The apostle’s affliction was bound up with their movement from alienation toward glory. What looked shameful in the Roman world had become an instrument in God’s saving purpose.

No equivalence should be drawn between Paul’s sufferings and Christ’s sacrifice. Jesus alone bore sin and accomplished atonement. Paul suffered as a witness to that finished work, not as a second redeemer. His endurance served the gospel because it kept the message moving through opposition.

The verse reorients Christian courage. Visible success is not the only evidence of divine faithfulness, and suffering is not proof that a ministry has failed. The imprisoned apostle could still illuminate the mystery, strengthen churches, and testify before earthly and heavenly powers. The gospel’s glory often advances through servants whose weakness makes the power of Christ more clearly seen.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to lose heart, become discouraged, or grow weary in doing what is right. Paul most likely asks the readers not to interpret his sufferings as evidence that the gospel has failed.

Paul’s faithful suffering served the mission through which the Gentiles received salvation and the hope of future glory. His afflictions were not themselves atoning but were endured in bringing Christ’s saving message to them.

verses.bibleText: For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the long explanation of his ministry, Paul returns to the prayer begun in verse 1. “For this cause” now gathers up the whole argument: God has reconciled Jews and Gentiles, formed them into one household, revealed His purpose through the gospel, and made the church a witness before the heavenly powers. Paul therefore prays that the believers will inwardly experience the reality already granted to them in Christ.

Kneeling expresses the intensity of the request. Bold access to God does not eliminate reverence. The person who knows God as Father may speak freely and still bow in humble recognition of His majesty and authority.

The KJV identifies God as “the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This Father-Son relationship does not weaken Christ’s full deity or imply that the Son is a created being. Ephesians has already placed Christ above every created power and associated Him with the divine work of creation, redemption, and universal rule. The language distinguishes the Father and the Son while affirming their united saving work.

The prayer is Trinitarian in movement. Paul bows before the Father, asks for strengthening through the Spirit, and desires that Christ dwell powerfully in the believers. Christian prayer enters the Father’s presence through the Son and depends upon the Spirit’s enabling presence.

wordNotes.term: bow my knees — κάμπτω τὰ γόνατά μου (kamptō ta gonata mou)
wordNotes.explanation: Standing was a common posture for prayer, so the reference to kneeling conveys particular earnestness, humility, and submission before God.

verses.bibleText: Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Father and family are joined by a deliberate play on words. Every family, clan, or created order in heaven and on earth receives its name from the Father. Naming is more than attaching a verbal label. It signifies that God gives creatures their existence, assigns their place, and exercises rightful authority over them.

The KJV’s “whole family” harmonizes with the preceding picture of Jews and Gentiles brought into one household. Those who were strangers have been adopted through Christ and now belong to one Father. No earthly ancestry can provide a higher spiritual rank within this family.

The Greek may also be understood as “every family,” widening the thought to all created orders in heaven and on earth. The Father to whom Paul prays is not a local deity competing with the spiritual powers familiar to the ancient world. He is Creator and sovereign over every visible and invisible order. The powers that threaten believers remain named, bounded, and ultimately judged by Him.

This language does not teach that every creature automatically enjoys saving sonship. God is Father of believers by adoption in Christ in a special covenantal sense. Nor does “the family in heaven” require the conclusion that deceased human beings are living consciously there. The expression naturally includes heavenly beings and created orders; the resurrection hope of the dead must be established from passages that address that subject directly.

Paul’s point is pastoral and theological. The Father who hears the prayer is both intimately near to His children and universally sovereign over creation. The church’s unity rests in a Fatherhood greater than every human family division, and its security rests in the authority of the One from whom all created powers receive their very name.

wordNotes.term: the whole family — πᾶσα πατριά (pasa patria)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase can be rendered “every family” or “every clan.” The KJV’s “whole family” fittingly emphasizes the unity of God’s household, while the Greek also affirms that every created order derives its identity and existence from the Father.
In biblical thought, naming can express creation, authority, and the assigning of identity. Every earthly and heavenly order remains dependent upon God and subject to His rule.

verses.bibleText: That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first explicit request concerns inward strength. Paul does not ask first that the prison doors open, hostile authorities disappear, or the believers gain social influence. He asks that God strengthen them where discouragement, fear, temptation, and unbelief exert their deepest pressure.

God grants this strength “according to the riches of his glory.” Paul does not picture God giving reluctantly from a limited supply. The measure of the gift is the abundance of God’s own majestic power—the power already displayed when He raised Christ from the dead and exalted Him above every hostile authority.

The means of strengthening is “his Spirit.” Moral courage is not manufactured by repeating optimistic thoughts or relying upon natural willpower. The Holy Spirit applies God’s power to the interior life, producing confidence in the gospel, perseverance under suffering, resistance to sin, and the capacity to love across difficult boundaries.

“The inner man” describes the inward dimension of the whole person. Paul can contrast it with the outward body that is subject to weakness, suffering, aging, and death. The phrase should not be turned into a doctrine of a naturally immortal soul living independently within the body. The biblical hope remains the resurrection of the whole person. Here the concern is that the mind, will, conscience, and affections be renewed by the Spirit even while outward circumstances remain difficult.

Such strength is necessary because theological knowledge alone does not guarantee spiritual stability. The Ephesians may understand that Christ has triumphed and still feel afraid. Paul prays that revealed truth will become inward fortitude. God’s power must move from confession into character, enabling believers to stand faithfully until the promises received in Christ reach their final fulfillment.

wordNotes.term: strengthened with might — κραταιωθῆναι δυνάμει (krataiōthēnai dynamei)
wordNotes.explanation: The wording describes being made inwardly strong with divine power. The emphasis is upon spiritual courage, stability, and endurance rather than physical force or worldly dominance.

The phrase denotes the inward person—the mind, will, affections, conscience, and moral-spiritual life. It does not identify a naturally immortal, independently conscious entity separable from the whole person.

verses.bibleText: That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The desired inward strength has a Christ-centered result: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith.” Paul is addressing people who have already believed the gospel, received the Spirit, and been united with Christ. He is not suggesting that Christ has been entirely absent. He prays that Christ’s presence will become settled, governing, and deeply effective within them.

The heart in biblical thought is the center of thought, desire, decision, and allegiance. Christ dwelling there means more than emotional warmth. His truth reshapes judgment, His love redirects desire, and His lordship governs the will. Every inner room is opened to Him rather than carefully reserving areas for pride, resentment, fear, or secret sin.

This indwelling occurs “by faith.” The Christian life continues on the same basis on which it began: trusting dependence upon Christ. Faith receives His promises, yields to His authority, and relies upon the Spirit rather than attempting spiritual maturity through self-sufficient effort.

The risen Lord remains personally active in the heavenly realm, where He ministers for His people on the basis of His once-for-all sacrifice. His dwelling in believers should therefore not be imagined as a physical relocation of His glorified body. Christ makes His presence effective in His people through the Holy Spirit. The Father grants power, the Spirit strengthens, and Christ dwells—distinct personal activity within one divine saving work.

Paul then combines two images. Believers are “rooted” like a living plant and “grounded” like a stable building. Love is both soil and foundation. The immediate context points especially to God’s love revealed through Christ, which then creates love among believers. A church trying to build unity upon shared culture, institutional pressure, or fear may remain outwardly organized while inwardly fragile. Only the love displayed at the cross can nourish and support the new humanity Christ has created.

Rootedness suggests continued growth; grounding suggests stability. Christian maturity needs both. Love prevents firmness from becoming harshness and growth from becoming restless novelty. Christ’s settled rule produces a people who remain secure in grace and increasingly reflect His character.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb commonly describes settling down or making a home. The prayer is for Christ’s presence and rule to become established and effective throughout the believers’ inward life, not merely for a passing religious impression.

wordNotes.term: rooted and grounded — ἐρριζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι (errizōmenoi kai tethemeliōmenoi)
wordNotes.explanation: Paul combines agricultural and architectural images. Love is both the nourishing soil in which Christian life grows and the stable foundation upon which the believing community is built.

verses.bibleText: May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Spiritual strength is needed in order to comprehend. The love of Christ is not grasped merely by natural intelligence, and the mystery of God is not mastered through detached analysis. The Spirit strengthens the inward person so that revealed truth may be received with the whole life.

Paul lists four dimensions—breadth, length, depth, and height—without immediately naming what they measure. The language has been connected with the cross, the church as God’s temple, the promised inheritance, the dimensions of the universe, and the vast plan of God. The references to love immediately before and after the list make the love of Christ the most likely primary subject. Yet the broader mystery remains in view: Christ’s love is displayed in God’s many-sided wisdom, gathering diverse people into one body and moving creation toward unity under Him.

No precise allegory should be imposed upon each dimension. Paul does not explain that breadth means one doctrine and height another. The cumulative force is immensity. Christ’s love extends beyond every boundary by which fallen humanity restricts grace. It reaches people formerly far off, persists through the ages, descends into the depths of human misery and death, and raises believers into fellowship with the exalted Lord. These are illustrations of the whole picture rather than inspired definitions of the individual measurements.

Comprehension occurs “with all saints.” No isolated believer or single culture possesses the whole perspective. Jewish and Gentile believers, men and women, rich and poor, and people from every nation perceive dimensions of Christ’s grace together that remain obscured when one group treats its experience as complete. The reconciled church is not only the object of Christ’s love; it is the community within which that love becomes increasingly intelligible.

The phrase therefore opposes both individualistic spirituality and secret religious elitism. The mystery is understood in the communion of all God’s people. As believers receive, practice, forgive, serve, and suffer together in Christ’s love, they begin to grasp what no solitary mind could contain.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb can mean to grasp, seize, or understand. Paul pictures believers becoming spiritually strong enough to lay hold of a reality too vast for unaided human understanding.

wordNotes.term: breadth, and length, and depth, and height — πλάτος καὶ μῆκος καὶ ὕψος καὶ βάθος (platos kai mēkos kai hypsos kai bathos)
wordNotes.explanation: The four dimensions portray immeasurable vastness. Their immediate object is most likely Christ’s love, though they also echo the cosmic scope of God’s mystery and wisdom. The text does not assign a fixed symbolic meaning to each dimension.

verses.bibleText: And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s paradox is intentional: believers are to know a love that surpasses knowledge. Christ’s love is not unknowable, for the gospel makes it visible. It is seen in His incarnation, His life among sinners, His self-giving death, His resurrection, and His continuing ministry on behalf of His people. Yet every genuine discovery reveals that more remains beyond the limits of human comprehension.

The knowledge Paul seeks is neither anti-intellectual nor merely academic. The mind must understand the gospel, but the whole person must also receive and inhabit its reality. A person may define grace correctly while continuing to live under fear, bitterness, or spiritual superiority. Paul prays for knowledge that reaches the heart, steadies the conscience, and produces love within the community.

Christ’s cross supplies the decisive measure. He loved those who were dead in sins, hostile to God, and divided from one another. His sacrifice was complete and offered once for all. His risen life and heavenly intercession reveal that the love displayed at Calvary has not diminished. Believers approach the Father through a living Saviour who continues to represent, cleanse, guide, and sustain them.

The final purpose is “that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.” The expression cannot mean absorption into God’s essence or elevation of human beings into independent deity. The Creator-creature distinction remains. Christ alone possesses the fullness of deity bodily. Believers are filled as recipients who increasingly reflect God’s holiness, love, truth, and unity.

The wording points toward maturity. Ephesians 4:13 will speak of reaching the measure of the stature of Christ’s fullness. God intends to restore in His people what sin has disfigured, forming a community that bears His character. This filling is present and progressive through the Spirit, corporate as the church grows in love, and future in its completion when Christ returns, raises His people, and brings them into perfected life.

The sequence of the prayer is important. The Spirit strengthens; Christ dwells; believers become rooted in love; the community comprehends Christ’s immeasurable love; and the church grows toward divine fullness. Holiness is not produced by fear-driven effort. It grows from the settled presence of Christ and the increasingly profound knowledge of His love.

wordNotes.term: know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge — γνῶναι τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς γνώσεως ἀγάπην τοῦ Χριστοῦ (gnōnai tēn hyperballousan tēs gnōseōs agapēn tou Christou)
wordNotes.explanation: Paul deliberately joins knowing with what surpasses knowledge. Christ’s love can be truly known through revelation and experience, but it can never be exhaustively comprehended.

wordNotes.term: fulness of God — πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ (plērōma tou theou)
wordNotes.explanation: The fullness of God is the goal of mature conformity to God’s holy and loving character, individually and corporately. It does not mean that creatures become divine in essence or share God’s infinite being.

verses.bibleText: Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The prayer rises into praise. Paul has asked for inward strength, Christ’s settled presence, comprehension of immeasurable love, and growth toward God’s fullness. These requests exceed human ability, but they do not exceed God’s. He is able to do “exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think.”

The language deliberately overflows. God can do what His people ask, what they can imagine but fail to ask, and far beyond the total range of both prayer and thought. Human expectation cannot set the outer boundary of divine power.

Its horizon is established by the prayer that precedes it, not by the uncontrolled ambitions of the fallen heart. The promise is not a guarantee that every desire for wealth, influence, comfort, or spectacular intervention will be granted. Paul himself remains imprisoned while writing it. God’s exceeding power may be displayed by sustaining faith under suffering, reconciling enemies, overcoming sin, and forming Christlike character rather than by removing every hardship.

The power is already “working in us.” Paul does not direct attention only to future miracles or external providences. The Spirit’s inward work is itself evidence of resurrection power. Every movement from hatred toward love, from fear toward faith, from selfishness toward service, and from division toward unity testifies that the power which raised Christ is active among His people.

Prayer therefore rests on more than abstract omnipotence. The God who can do beyond imagination has already begun His work within the church. Present grace becomes the pledge of completion. He is able to preserve His people, mature them in love, and finally raise them from death when Christ returns. The distance between their present weakness and their promised fullness is vast, but it is not greater than His power.

wordNotes.explanation: The heavily intensified adverb means exceedingly beyond measure or infinitely more. Paul piles up language because ordinary comparison seems inadequate for God’s ability.

wordNotes.term: the power that worketh in us — δύναμις ἡ ἐνεργουμένη ἐν ἡμῖν (dynamis hē energoumenē en hēmin)
wordNotes.explanation: God’s power is already active within His people through the Spirit. It is the resurrection power previously displayed in Christ and now producing faith, holiness, endurance, love, and unity in the church.

verses.bibleText: Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The doxology reaches its goal in the glory of God. Everything described in the first three chapters—election in Christ, redemption through His blood, resurrection life, reconciliation, the Spirit’s presence, the revealed mystery, access to the Father, and inward transformation—originates in God and returns in praise to Him.

Glory is manifested “in the church by Christ Jesus.” The church possesses no independent brilliance and cannot make itself the object of worship. It glorifies God because it is Christ’s body, created by His sacrifice, sustained by His Spirit, and governed by His lordship. A reconciled community drawn from divided peoples becomes visible evidence of God’s grace and wisdom.

Christ remains the mediating center. God’s glory is revealed supremely in Him, and the church reflects that glory only through union with Him. The church must therefore resist both contempt for the community Christ purchased and institutional pride that exalts the church above its Lord. Christ is the Head; the church is His dependent body.

“Throughout all ages, world without end” carries the praise beyond the present generation. The church’s existence is not a temporary response to a passing historical problem. God’s redeemed people will continue as the fruit of Christ’s work when the present order of sin and death has ended. Those who sleep in death will be raised at Christ’s return, the living faithful will be transformed, and the united community will glorify God in the restored creation.

The eternal future will not exhaust the riches announced in this chapter. Generation after generation and age after age, the redeemed will continue to discover the wisdom of God and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. “Amen” seals Paul’s praise with conviction. The God who began this purpose before the ages, accomplished it in Christ, and works by His Spirit in the church will receive glory without end.

wordNotes.term: throughout all ages, world without end — εἰς πάσας τὰς γενεὰς τοῦ αἰῶνος τῶν αἰώνων (eis pasas tas geneas tou aiōnos tōn aiōnōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The expansive phrase speaks of every generation through the age composed of all ages. The KJV’s “world without end” captures its declaration that God’s glory will continue forever.
Derived from a word associated with firmness and truth, “Amen” expresses heartfelt agreement: what has been spoken is true, and may its praise be fully realized.
